arXiv:1406.5233v4 [math.AP] 02 Oct 2014

Construction of a stable blow-up solution for a class of strongly perturbed semilinear heat equations

V. T. Nguyen and H. Zaag
Université Paris 13, Sorbonne Paris Cité,
LAGA, CNRS (UMR 7539), F-93430, Villetaneuse, France. Note: This author is supported by the ERC Advanced Grant no. 291214, BLOWDISOL and by the ANR project ANAÉ ref. ANR-13-BS01-0010-03.
Abstract

We construct a solution for a class of strongly perturbed semilinear heat equations which blows up in finite time with a prescribed blow-up profile. The construction relies on the reduction of the problem to a finite dimensional one and the use of index theory to conclude.

Keywords: Blow-up profile, finite-time blow-up, stability, semilinear heat equations.

1 Introduction

We are interested in the following nonlinear parabolic equation:

{ut=Δ​u+|u|p−1​u+h⁡(u),u⁡(0)=u0∈L∞​(ℝn),\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}&=&\Delta u+|u|^{p-1}u+h(u),\\ u(0)&=&u_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),\end{array}\right. (1)

where uu is defined for (x,t)∈ℝn×[0,T)(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T), 1<p1<p and p<n+2n−2p<\frac{n+2}{n-2} if n≥3n\geq 3, the function hh is in 𝒞1​(ℝ,ℝ)\mathcal{C}^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) satisfying

j=0,1,|h(j)​(z)|≤M⁡(|z|p−jloga⁡(2+z2)+1)​with​a>1,M>0,j=0,1,\;\;|h^{(j)}(z)|\leq M\left(\dfrac{|z|^{p-j}}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})}+1\right)\;\;\;\text{with}\;\;a>1,\;M>0, (2)

or

h⁡(z)=μ​|z|p−1​zloga⁡(2+z2)​with​a>0,μ∈ℝ.h(z)=\mu\dfrac{|z|^{p-1}z}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})}\;\;\;\text{with}\;\;a>0,\;\mu\in\mathbb{R}. (3)

By standard results, the Cauchy problem for equation (1) can be solved in L∞​(ℝn)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). The solution u⁡(t)u(t) of (1) would exist either on [0,+∞)[0,+\infty) (global existence) or only on [0,T)[0,T), with 0<T<+∞0<T<+\infty. In this case, we say that u⁡(t)u(t) blows up in finite time TT, namely

limt→T‖u⁡(t)‖L∞​(ℝn)=+∞.\lim_{t\to T}\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}=+\infty.

Here TT is called the blow-up time, and a point x0∈ℝnx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is called a blow-up point if and only if there exist (xn,tn)→(x0,T)(x_{n},t_{n})\to(x_{0},T) such that |u⁡(xn,tn)|→+∞|u(x_{n},t_{n})|\to+\infty as n→+∞n\to+\infty. In this paper, we are interested in the finite time blow-up for equation (1).

When h≡0h\equiv 0, the blow-up result for equation (1) is largely well-understood. The existence of blow-up solutions has been proved by several authors (see Fujita [7], Ball [1], Levine [13]). We have a lots of results concerning the asymptotic blow-up behavior, locally near a given blow-up point (see Giga and Kohn [10], Weissler [25], Filippas, Kohn and Liu [5], [6], Herrero and Velázquez [11], [12], [23], [24], Merle and Zaag [17], [18], [19]). The notion of asymptotic profile appears also in various papers (see Bricmont and Kupiainen [3], Merle and Zaag [16], Berger and Kohn [2], Nguyen [20] for numerical studies).

Given bb a blow-up point of uu, we study the behavior of uu near the singularity (b,T)(b,T) through the following similarity variables introduced by Giga and Kohn [8, 9, 10]:

y=x−bT−t,s=−log⁡(T−t),wb​(y,s)=(T−t)1p−1​u​(x,t),y=\frac{x-b}{\sqrt{T-t}},\quad s=-\log(T-t),\quad w_{b}(y,s)=(T-t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}u(x,t), (4)

and wbw_{b} satisfies for all (y,s)∈ℝn×[−logT,+∞)(y,s)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[-\log T,+\infty),

∂swb=(Δ−y2⋅∇+1)wb−pp−1wb+|wb|p−1wb+e−p​sp−1h(esp−1wb).\partial_{s}w_{b}=(\Delta-\frac{y}{2}\cdot\nabla+1)w_{b}-\frac{p}{p-1}w_{b}+|w_{b}|^{p-1}w_{b}+e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}w_{b}\right). (5)

In [21], the author showed that if wbw_{b} does not approach ϕ\phi exponentially fast, where ϕ\phi is the positive solution of the associated ordinary differential equation of equation (5),

ϕs=−ϕp−1+ϕp+e−p​sp−1​h​(esp−1​ϕ)such thatϕ⁡(s)→κass→+∞,\phi_{s}=-\frac{\phi}{p-1}+\phi^{p}+e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\phi)\quad\text{such that}\quad\phi(s)\to\kappa\quad\text{as}\quad s\to+\infty, (6)

then the solution uu of (1) would approach an explicit universal profile as follows:

(T−t)1p−1​u​(b+z​(T−t)​|log⁡(T−t)|,t)→f⁡(z)ast→T,(T-t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}u(b+z\sqrt{(T-t)|\log(T-t)|},t)\to f(z)\quad\text{as}\quad t\to T, (7)

in Ll​o​c∞L_{loc}^{\infty} and in the case a>1a>1, where

f⁡(z)=κ​(1+cp​|z|2)−1p−1,with​cp=p−14​p.f(z)=\kappa\left(1+c_{p}|z|^{2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}},\quad\text{with}\;\;c_{p}=\frac{p-1}{4p}. (8)

The goal of this work is to show that the behavior (7) does occur. More precisely, we construct a blow-up solution of equation (1) satisfying the behavior described in (7). This is our main result:

Theorem 1 (Existence of a blow-up solution for equation (1) with the description of its profile).

There exists T>0T>0 such that equation (1) has a solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) in ℝn×[0,T)\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T) satisfying:
𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i)i) the solution uu blows up in finite-time TT at the point b=0b=0,
𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i​i)ii)

‖(T−t)1p−1u(⋅T−t,t)−f(⋅|log⁡(T−t)|)‖W1,∞​(ℝn)≤C|log⁡(T−t)|ϱ,\left\|(T-t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}u(\cdot\sqrt{T-t},t)-f\left(\frac{\cdot}{\sqrt{|\log(T-t)|}}\right)\right\|_{W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq\frac{C}{|\log(T-t)|^{\varrho}}, (9)

for all ϱ∈(0,ν)\varrho\in(0,\nu) with ν=min⁡{a−1,12}\nu=\min\{a-1,\frac{1}{2}\} in the case (2) and ν=min⁡{a,12}\nu=\min\{a,\frac{1}{2}\} in the case (3), CC is some positive constant and ff is defined in (8).
𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i​i​i)iii) There exists u∗∈𝒞⁡(ℝn∖{0},ℝ)u_{*}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\},\mathbb{R}) such that u​(x,t)→u∗​(x)u(x,t)\to u_{*}(x) as t→Tt\to T uniformly on compact subsets of ℝn∖{0}\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}, where

u∗​(x)∼(8​p​|log⁡|x||(p−1)2​|x|2)1p−1asx→0.u_{*}(x)\sim\left(\frac{8p|\log|x||}{(p-1)^{2}|x|^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}\quad\text{as}\quad x\to 0.
Remark 1.

Note that 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i)i) directly follows from 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i​i)ii). Indeed, 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i​i)ii) implies that u⁡(0,t)∼κ​(T−t)−1p−1→+∞u(0,t)\sim\kappa(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\to+\infty as t→Tt\to T, which means that uu blows up in finite-time TT at the point 00. From 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i​i​i)iii), we see that uu blows up only at the point b=0b=0.

Remark 2.

Note that the profile ff is the same as in the nonlinear heat equation without the perturbation (h≡0h\equiv 0), see Bricmont and Kupiainen [3], Merle and Zaag [16].
The estimate (9) holds in W1,∞W^{1,\infty} and uniformly in z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. In the previous work, Ebde and Zaag [4] gives such a uniform convergence in the case hh involving a nonlinear gradient term. In fact, the convergence in W1,∞W^{1,\infty} comes from a parabolic regularity estimate for equation (5) (see Proposition 5 below). Dealing with the case h≡0h\equiv 0, Bricmont and Kupiainen [3], Merle and Zaag [16] also give such a uniform convergence but only in L∞​(ℝn)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). In most papers, the same kind convergence is proved, but only uniformly on a smaller subsets, |z|≤K​|log⁡(T−t)||z|\leq K\sqrt{|\log(T-t)|} (see Velázquez [23]).

The proof of Theorem 1 bases on techniques developed by Bricmont and Kupiainen in [3] and Merle and Zaag in [16] for the semilinear heat equation

ut=Δ​u+|u|p−1​u.u_{t}=\Delta u+|u|^{p-1}u. (10)

Note that the perturbation term hh certainly impacts on the construction of solutions of (1) satisfying (9). This causes some crucial modifications in [16] in order to totally control the term hh. Although these modifications do not affect the general framework developed in [16], they lay in 3 crucial places:
- We modify the profile around which we study equation (5), so that we go beyond the order 1sa\frac{1}{s^{a}} generated by the perturbation term. Indeed, for small a>0a>0 and with the same profile as in [16], the order 1sa\frac{1}{s^{a}} will become too strong and will not allow us to close our estimates. See Section 2 below, particularly definition (12), which enables us to reach the order 1sa+1\frac{1}{s^{a+1}}.
- In order to handle the order 1sa+1\frac{1}{s^{a+1}}, we need to modify the definition of the shrinking set near the profile. See Section 3 and particularly Proposition 3 below.
- A sharp understanding of the dynamics of the linearized operator of (5) around the profile (12), and which allows to handle the new definition of the shrinking set. See Lemma (7) below.

For that reason, we will stress only the main parts of the proof of Theorem 1 and put forward the novelties of our argument. In particular, the proof relies on the understanding of the dynamics of the self-similar version of equation (5) around the profile (8). Following the work by Merle and Zaag [16], the proof will be divided into 2 steps:
- In the first step, we reduce the problem to a finite-dimensional problem: we will show that it is enough to control a finite-dimensional variable in order to control the solution near the profile.
- In the second step, we proceed by contradiction to solve the finite-dimensional problem and conclude using index theory.

We would like to mention that Masmoudi and Zaag [14] adapted the method of [16] for the following Ginzburg-Landau equation:

ut=(1+ı​β)​Δ​u+(1+ı​δ)​|u|p−1​u,u_{t}=(1+\imath\beta)\Delta u+(1+\imath\delta)|u|^{p-1}u, (11)

where p−δ2−β​δ​(p+1)>0p-\delta^{2}-\beta\delta(p+1)>0 and u:ℝn×[0,T)→ℂu:\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T)\to\mathbb{C}. Note that the case β=0\beta=0 and δ∈ℝ\delta\in\mathbb{R} small has been studied earlier by Zaag [26].
In [22], Nouaili and Zaag successfully used the method of [16] for the following complex valued semilinear heat equation:

ut=Δ​u+u2,u_{t}=\Delta u+u^{2},

where u⁡(t):x∈ℝn→ℂu(t):x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}.

As in [16], [26] and [14], it is possible to make the interpretation of the finite-dimensional variable in terms of the blow-up time and the blow-up point. This allows us to derive the stability of the profile ff in Theorem 1 with respect to perturbations in the initial data. More precisely, we have the following:

Theorem 2 (Stability of the solution constructed in Theorem 1).

Let us denote by u^​(x,t)\hat{u}(x,t) the solution constructed in Theorem 1 and by T^\hat{T} its blow-up time. Then, there exists a neighborhood 𝒱0\mathcal{V}_{0} of u^​(x,0)\hat{u}(x,0) in W1,∞W^{1,\infty} such that for any u0∈𝒱0u_{0}\in\mathcal{V}_{0}, equation (1) has a unique solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) with initial data u0u_{0}, and u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) blows up in finite time T⁡(u0)T(u_{0}) at one single blow-up point b⁡(u0)b(u_{0}). Moreover, estimate (7) is satisfied by u⁡(x−b,t)u(x-b,t) and

T(u0)→T^,b(u0)→0as u0→u^0 in W1,∞​(ℝn).T(u_{0})\to\hat{T},\quad b(u_{0})\to 0\quad\text{as $u_{0}\to\hat{u}_{0}$ in $W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$}.
Remark 3.

We will not give the proof of Theorem 2 because the stability result follows from the reduction to a finite dimensional case as in [16] with the same proof. Hence, we only prove the reduction and refer to [16] for the stability. Note that from the parabolic regularity, our stability result holds in the larger space L∞​(ℝn)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).

2 Formulation of the problem

As in [16], [3], we give the proof in one dimension (n=1n=1). The proof remains the same for higher dimensions (n≥2n\geq 2). We would like to find u0u_{0} initial data such that the solution uu of equation (1) blows up in finite time TT and satisfies the estimate (9). Using similarity variables (4), this is equivalent to finding s0>0s_{0}>0 and w0​(y)≡w⁡(y,s0)w_{0}(y)\equiv w(y,s_{0}) such that the solution ww of equation (5) with initial data w0w_{0} satisfies

lims→+∞‖w⁡(y,s)−f⁡(ys)‖W1,∞=0,\lim_{s\to+\infty}\|w(y,s)-f(\frac{y}{\sqrt{s}})\|_{W^{1,\infty}}=0,

where ff is given in (8).
In order to prove this, we will not linearize equation (5) around f+κ2​p​sf+\frac{\kappa}{2ps} as in [16]. We will instead introduce

q=w−φ,whereφ=ϕ⁡(s)κ​(f⁡(ys)+κ2​p​s),q=w-\varphi,\quad\text{where}\quad\varphi=\frac{\phi(s)}{\kappa}\left(f(\frac{y}{\sqrt{s}})+\frac{\kappa}{2ps}\right), (12)

with ϕ\phi and ff are introduced in (6) and (8). Then, the problem is reduced to constructing a function qq such that

lims→+∞‖q⁡(y,s)‖W1,∞=0\lim_{s\to+\infty}\|q(y,s)\|_{W^{1,\infty}}=0

and qq is a solution of the following equation for all (y,s)∈ℝ×[s0,+∞)(y,s)\in\mathbb{R}\times[s_{0},+\infty),

qs=(ℒ+V)​q+B⁡(q)+R⁡(y,s)+N⁡(y,s),q_{s}=(\mathcal{L}+V)q+B(q)+R(y,s)+N(y,s), (13)

where ℒ=Δ−y2⋅∇+1\mathcal{L}=\Delta-\frac{y}{2}\cdot\nabla+1 and

V⁡(y,s)\displaystyle V(y,s) =p⁡(φ​(y,s)p−1−1p−1)+ı​e−s​h′​(esp−1​φ),\displaystyle=p\left(\varphi(y,s)^{p-1}-\frac{1}{p-1}\right)+\imath e^{-s}h^{\prime}(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\varphi), (14)
B⁡(q)\displaystyle B(q) =|φ+q|p−1​(φ+q)−φp−p​φp−1​q,\displaystyle=|\varphi+q|^{p-1}(\varphi+q)-\varphi^{p}-p\varphi^{p-1}q, (15)
R⁡(y,s)\displaystyle R(y,s) =−φs+Δ​φ−y2⋅∇φ−φp−1+φp+e−p​sp−1​h​(esp−1​φ),\displaystyle=-\varphi_{s}+\Delta\varphi-\frac{y}{2}\cdot\nabla\varphi-\frac{\varphi}{p-1}+\varphi^{p}+e^{\frac{-ps}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\varphi\right), (16)
N⁡(q,s)\displaystyle N(q,s) =e−p​sp−1​[h⁡(esp−1​(φ+q))−h⁡(esp−1​φ)−ı​esp−1​h′​(esp−1​φ)​q],\displaystyle=e^{\frac{-ps}{p-1}}\left[h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}(\varphi+q)\right)-h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\varphi\right)-\imath e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}h^{\prime}\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\varphi\right)q\right], (17)

with ı=0\imath=0 in the case (2) and ı=1\imath=1 in the case (3).

One can remark that we don’t linearize (5) around φ~=f⁡(ys)+κ2​p​s\tilde{\varphi}=f(\frac{y}{\sqrt{s}})+\frac{\kappa}{2ps} as in the case of equation (10) treated in [16]. In fact, if we do the same, we may obtain some terms like 1sa\frac{1}{s^{a}} coming from the strong perturbation hh in equation (5), and we may not be able to control these terms in the case a<3a<3. To extend the range of aa, we multiply the factor ϕ⁡(s)κ\frac{\phi(s)}{\kappa} to φ~\tilde{\varphi} in order to go beyond the order 1sa\frac{1}{s^{a}} and reach at the order 1sa+1\frac{1}{s^{a+1}}. Linearizing around φ\varphi given in (12) is a major novelty in our approach.

In following analysis, we will use the following integral form of equation (13): for each s≥σ≥s0s\geq\sigma\geq s_{0}:

q⁡(s)=𝒦⁡(s,σ)​q​(σ)+∫σs𝒦⁡(s,τ)​[B⁡(q⁡(τ))+R⁡(τ)+N⁡(q⁡(τ),τ)]​𝑑τ,q(s)=\mathcal{K}(s,\sigma)q(\sigma)+\int_{\sigma}^{s}\mathcal{K}(s,\tau)\left[B(q(\tau))+R(\tau)+N(q(\tau),\tau)\right]d\tau, (18)

where 𝒦\mathcal{K} is the fundamental solution of the linear operator ℒ+V\mathcal{L}+V defined for each σ>0\sigma>0 and for each s≥σs\geq\sigma,

∂s𝒦⁡(s,σ)=(ℒ+V)​𝒦​(s,σ),𝒦⁡(σ,σ)=I​d​e​n​t​i​t​y.\partial_{s}\mathcal{K}(s,\sigma)=(\mathcal{L}+V)\mathcal{K}(s,\sigma),\quad\mathcal{K}(\sigma,\sigma)=Identity. (19)

The operator ℒ\mathcal{L} is self-adjoint in Lρ2​(ℝn)L^{2}_{\rho}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), where Lρ2L^{2}_{\rho} is the weighted L2L^{2} space associated with the weight ρ\rho defined by

ρ⁡(y)=(14​π)n/2​e−|y|24.\rho(y)=\left(\frac{1}{4\pi}\right)^{n/2}e^{-\frac{|y|^{2}}{4}}.

Hm​(y)=hm1​(y1)​…​hmn​(yn),where hm is defined in (20).H_{m}(y)=h_{m_{1}}(y_{1})\dots h_{m_{n}}(y_{n}),\quad\text{where $h_{m}$ is defined in \eqref{equ:eigenfu1}.} (21)

OPENi)i) V⁡(⋅,s)→0V(\cdot,s)\to 0 in Lρ2L^{2}_{\rho} as s→+∞s\to+\infty. In particular, the effect of VV on the bounded sets or in the "blow-up" region (|y|≤K​s|y|\leq K\sqrt{s}) is regarded as a perturbation of the effect of ℒ\mathcal{L}.

3 Proof of the existence of a blow-up solution with the given blow-up profile

In this section, we use the framework developed in [16] in order to prove Theorem 1. We proceed in 4 steps:
- In the first step, we define a shrinking set VA​(s)V_{A}(s) and translate our goal of making q⁡(s)q(s) go to 00 in L∞​(ℝ)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) in terms of belonging to VA​(s)V_{A}(s). We also exhibit a two parameter initial data family for equation (13) whose coordinates are very small (with respect to the requirements of VA​(s)V_{A}(s)), except the two first q0q_{0} and q1q_{1}. Note that the set VA​(s)V_{A}(s) is different from the corresponding one in [16], and this makes the second major novelty of our work, in addition to the modification of the profile in (12).
- In the second step, using the spectral properties of equation (13), we reduce our goal from the control of q⁡(s)q(s) (an infinite dimensional variable) in VA​(s)V_{A}(s) to the control of its two first components (q0​(s),q1​(s))(q_{0}(s),q_{1}(s)) (a two-dimensional variable) in [−As1+ν,As1+ν]2\left[-\frac{A}{s^{1+\nu}},\frac{A}{s^{1+\nu}}\right]^{2} with ν>0\nu>0.
- In the third step, we solve the local in time Cauchy problem for equation (13).
- In the last step, we solve the finite dimensional problem using index theory and conclude the proof of Theorem 1.

In what follows, the constant CC denotes a universal one independent of variables, only depending upon constants of the problems such as aa, pp, MM, μ\mu and KK in (23).

3.2 Reduction to a finite dimensional problem

We are going to the crucial step of the proof of Theorem 1. In this step, we will show that through a priori estimates, the control of q⁡(s)q(s) in VAV_{A} reduces to the control of (q0,q1)​(s)(q_{0},q_{1})(s) in V^A​(s)\hat{V}_{A}(s). As presented in [16] (see also[26],[14]), we would like to emphasize that this step make the heart of the contribution. Even more, here lays another major contribution of ours, in the sense that we understand better the dynamics of the fundamental solution 𝒦⁡(s,σ)\mathcal{K}(s,\sigma) defined in (19). Our sharper estimates are given in Lemma 7 below. In fact all that we do is to rewrite the corresponding estimates of Bricmont and Kupiainen [3] without taking into account the particular form of the shrinking set they used. Furthermore, because of the difference in the definition (12) of φ\varphi and the difference in the definition of VAV_{A}, the proof is far from being an adaptation of the proof written in [16]. We therefore need some involved arguments to control the components of qq and conclude the reduction to a finite dimensional problem.

We mainly claim the following:

- if (d0,d1)(d_{0},d_{1}) is chosen so that (q0,q1)​(s0)∈V^A​(s0)(q_{0},q_{1})(s_{0})\in\hat{V}_{A}(s_{0}), and
- if for all s∈[s0,s1]s\in[s_{0},s_{1}], q​(s)∈VA​(s)q(s)\in V_{A}(s) and q⁡(s1)∈∂VA​(s1)q(s_{1})\in\partial V_{A}(s_{1}) for some s1≥s0s_{1}\geq s_{0}, then:

𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i​i)ii) (Transversality) there exists η0>0\eta_{0}>0 such that for all η∈(0,η0)\eta\in(0,\eta_{0}), (q0,q1)​(s1+η)∉∂V^A​(s1+η)\;(q_{0},q_{1})(s_{1}+\eta)\not\in\partial\hat{V}_{A}(s_{1}+\eta) (hence, q⁡(s1+η)∉VA​(s1+η)q(s_{1}+\eta)\not\in V_{A}(s_{1}+\eta)).

The proof follows the general ideas of [16] and we proceed in three steps:
- Step 1: we give a priori estimates on q⁡(s)q(s) in VA​(s)V_{A}(s): assume that for given A>0A>0 lager, λ>0\lambda>0 and an initial time s0≥σ2​(A,λ)≥1s_{0}\geq\sigma_{2}(A,\lambda)\geq 1, we have q​(s)∈VA​(s)q(s)\in V_{A}(s) for each s∈[τ,τ+λ]s\in[\tau,\tau+\lambda] where τ≥s0\tau\geq s_{0}, then using the integral form (18) of q⁡(s)q(s), we derive new bounds on q2​(s),q−​(s)q_{2}(s),q_{-}(s) and qe​(s)q_{e}(s) for s∈[τ,τ+λ]s\in[\tau,\tau+\lambda].
- Step 2: we show that these new bounds are better than those defining VA​(s)V_{A}(s). It then remains to control q0​(s)q_{0}(s) and q1​(s)q_{1}(s). This means that the problem is reduced to the control of a two dimensional variable (q0,q1)​(s)(q_{0},q_{1})(s) and we then conclude OPENi)i) of Proposition 6.

In view of the formula (18), we see that Lemma 7 will play an important role in deriving the new bounds on the components of q⁡(s)q(s) and making our proof simpler. The proof is essentially the same as in [3], but those estimates did not present explicitly the dependence on all the components of ψ⁡(σ)\psi(\sigma) which is less convenient for our analysis below. Because the proof is long and technical, we leave it to Appendix B. ∎

3.4 Deriving conclusion OPENi​i)ii) of Theorem 1

In this subsection, we derive conclusion OPENi​i)ii) of Theorem 1 using the previous subsections.
